name: Bianca Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a line of stamping presses at a plant that makes metal parts for washing machines and dryers: side panels, drum brackets, the back plates. A coil of steel goes in one end, the presses punch and bend it in stages, and finished panels come out the other. I'm the senior setter, so I change the dies, tune the pressure, and I'm on the pilot team for the new robot arm that moves panels between presses.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the robot pilot, if I'm honest. I use an AI assistant every day to look up fault codes and to write the little programs for the arm, and it's made me the person people come to. What wears me out is the money. We're paid a bit under the bigger plants, and Jonas has his own small garage, so some months he brings in plenty and some months almost nothing. With two kids and a mortgage, that's a lot of maths on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd keep showing people how to use it for the fiddly stuff. Online I'd probably post a picture of the robot arm with a caption like, still needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit bored. I like learning new stuff, and if it all stalls, I'm back to just changing dies. But my job's safe, and with money this tight, safe is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the robot pilot and ask to be made the plant's go-to person for it, with a pay bump. I'd also help Jonas set up an AI booking and diagnosis system for the garage, so he spends less time on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money's a lot of maths on the kitchen table. Walk me through a bad month.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March the garage had three customers not pay on time and the van's clutch went. We had about two hundred left after the mortgage. I sold my old bike online and we did a month of soup and bread. The kids thought it was a game, soup club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a pay bump of, say, a hundred a month mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean the bad months are just bad, not scary. We could put a bit by and stop holding our breath every time the van makes a noise.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a good tool, not a miracle, and keep showing people how to use it. Online I'd post a picture of the robot arm captioned 'still needs me'.
S0.think: I think I'd be a bit relieved and a bit bored, since I like learning new things. But my job's safe, and with money this tight, safe is good.
S0.do: Keeps working on the robot pilot and asks to be the plant's go-to person for it, with a pay rise. Helps her partner set up an AI booking and diagnosis system for his garage.
S0.quote: We did a month of soup and bread. The kids thought it was a game, soup club.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca is curious and already the go-to person on the robot pilot. Her household income swings because her partner is self-employed, which makes the thin cushion feel even thinner. She turned a bad month into 'soup club' for her kids, which says a lot about her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news if you're willing to learn. I'd tell the younger ones to get on the robot pilot now. Online I'd probably share some how-to videos, because people are scared when they don't need to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd come out ahead. Somebody has to set up and look after the robots, and I'm already doing it. The people who just feed parts in are the ones at risk, and I'd feel for them, but I'd be in a good spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the next phase of the robot rollout, and push for a team lead title and pay. I'd keep practising with the AI tools in the evenings, writing programs for the arm. On the side, I'd help Jonas add electric car repairs at the garage, because that's where cars are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. Calm about my own job, a little nervous for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the others you'd be nervous for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our press feeders. Six of them, mostly older men who've done the same job twenty years. One of them, Stan, taught me to change a die when I was twenty-four. If my robot rollout puts Stan out of a job, that's going to be an awkward lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get Stan onto my team as the safety checker. Somebody who knows how a press can hurt you is worth keeping. Whether management listens, I don't know.

S1.say: I'd say this is good news if you're willing to learn and tell younger workers to join the robot pilot now. Online I'd share how-to videos because people are scared when they don't need to be.
S1.think: I think I'd come out ahead because I'm already setting up and looking after the robots. The press feeders are at risk, and I'd feel for them.
S1.do: Asks to lead the next robot rollout with a team lead title and pay, and practises programming the arm in the evenings. Helps her partner add electric car repairs at his garage.
S1.feel: Excited and calm about her own job, a little nervous for others.
S1.quote: If my robot rollout puts Stan out of a job, that's going to be an awkward lunch.
S1.fieldNote: Bianca is the one bringing the robots in, and she knows it. Her discomfort about Stan, who trained her, is honest and specific. She thinks in two incomes, already steering her partner's garage toward electric cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough and we need practical help quickly, like bridging pay and help with mortgages. I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help anyone. And I'd keep sharing tips on how to use the tools while they're still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one frightens me. Two years means my robot skills are worth something for maybe a year, and then the AI programs the robots itself. And Jonas's garage would be hit too, because robot mechanics and self-driving cars that need less fixing. Both our incomes, at once, with nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard at overtime and offer to help other plants set up their robots on weekends, as paid contract work, while that's still a thing. Every spare bit goes into savings. We'd cut the second phone plan, the kids' trampoline club, and Jonas would sell the spare van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in the slow one you'd come out ahead. Why not here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in the slow one I'm ahead of the people behind me. In the fast one, the robots are ahead of all of us, including me. Being early only helps if there's a later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas say to each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas would say, we've had worse months. I'd say, not twenty-four of them in a row. Then we'd make a list. We're good at lists.

S2.say: I'd say it's going to be rough and we need practical help quickly, like bridging pay and mortgage help. I'd say it calmly because panic doesn't help.
S2.think: I think my robot skills would be worth something for about a year before AI programs robots itself. My partner's garage would be hit too, so both incomes go with nothing saved.
S2.do: Takes heavy overtime and paid weekend contract work setting up robots at other plants, putting every spare bit into savings. Cuts a phone plan and the kids' trampoline club, and her partner sells the spare van.
S2.quote: Being early only helps if there's a later.
S2.fieldNote: For Bianca the fast scenario turns her advantage upside down: being early is worth little if the wave is total. Her partner's garage makes the household doubly exposed. She stays calm in public but admits she'd be up at night doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people like me to move, and the company should help others move too. I'd push for training money and share what I know. I'd be one of the people running sessions in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I can do a lot. I'd get a proper qualification in robotics, maybe at the college, and try to get a job as an automation technician at a bigger company. But at the end, I'm not sure what's left. I'd at least want to have some savings by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd enrol in the robotics certificate part-time and use the AI tools to study. I'd do contract setups on weekends, maybe one a month, and save all of that. Jonas would retrain his garage toward electric cars and maybe robot repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. Like a race I think I can at least finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to make that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekends, mostly. Saturday mornings at the kids' football would go for a while, which I'd hate. Jonas would take them. It's a trade, two years of not seeing as much of them so they've got something later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualification and some money in the bank. With two years I'm just grabbing. With five I'm building. Even if the building gets knocked down at the end, at least we've got bricks.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for people like me to move, and the company should help others move too. I'd run training sessions in the canteen.
S3.think: I think I can get a robotics qualification and an automation technician job at a bigger company. I'm not sure what's left at the end, so I want savings by then.
S3.do: Enrols part-time in a robotics certificate in the first year and does about one paid weekend robot setup a month, saving all of it. Her partner shifts his garage toward electric cars and robot repair.
S3.feel: Anxious but excited, like a race she can at least finish.
S3.quote: Even if the building gets knocked down at the end, at least we've got bricks.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Bianca from grabbing to building, and she's clear-eyed that the end point may still knock it down. The cost she names is time with her kids on weekends. She keeps planning as a couple, with her partner's garage as the second leg.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get this right, so let's do it properly. Train people, help older workers, and don't leave towns like ours behind. I'd say it and I'd vote for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is plenty to build something. I could become a robotics technician, maybe even a trainer at the college. The end point still bothers me, but I'd have a decade of better pay and maybe some savings before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the robotics certificate. Within three years I'd want a technician job, even if it means a longer drive. Jonas would build the garage into electric and robot repair, and we'd try to save a thousand a year. And Freya would hear a lot from me about studying something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Freya to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where she understands the machines and the people. Maybe engineering, maybe teaching. She wants to be an influencer, which, well. I'd say, fine, and also learn how the camera works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in ten years that makes you nervous?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. With ten years, it's easy to think there's always time. I've seen people at work do that with every change. I'd have to keep myself honest.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this properly: train people, help older workers and don't leave towns like ours behind. I'd vote for that.
S4.think: I think ten years is plenty to build something, perhaps as a robotics technician or college trainer. The end point bothers me, but I'd have a decade of better pay and some savings first.
S4.do: Starts the robotics certificate this year and aims for a technician job within three years, even with a longer drive. Builds her partner's garage toward electric and robot repair, saves about a thousand a year, and steers her daughter toward useful study.
S4.quote: With ten years, it's easy to think there's always time.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Bianca's biggest worry is her own complacency rather than the money. She plans to move first and build a second career, with her partner reshaping the garage. Her advice to her daughter mixes humour with a practical push.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It hits both of us at once and turns my head start into nothing. What would help is bridging pay, something that tides families over for a year while they move, and cheap or free courses that you can do around shifts and kids.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who bring the robots in. I'd be the one setting up the arm that replaces Stan. That's a weird thing to carry home. Nobody asks how that feels.

headlineQuote: I'd be the one setting up the arm that replaces Stan. That's a weird thing to carry home.
portrait: Bianca Olsen is a 43-year-old senior setter at a metal stamping plant that makes washing machine parts, and the go-to person on its robot arm pilot. She uses an AI assistant every day, and her partner Jonas runs a small garage whose income swings month to month. She's calm in the first two scenarios and sees Steady Disruption as her chance to lead, though she feels for the older press feeders, especially Stan, who trained her. AGI in 2 years alarms her because it wipes out her head start and hits both household incomes. With 5 or 10 years she plans a robotics qualification and a technician job, and builds the garage toward electric and robot repair.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it hits both her and her partner at once and turns her head start into nothing.
whatWouldHelp: Bridging pay that tides families over for a year while they move, and cheap or free courses that fit around shifts and children.
